summary: This BCP gives a framework for developing and judging new congestion control algorithms, the rules that stop senders from overloading the network. It replaces the earlier guidance in RFC 5033 to reflect how the congestion control landscape has changed, with the aim of keeping the Internet stable across very different paths.

eli5.summary: When everyone rushes through one door, nobody gets through. This sets out the checklist a new "take turns" rule must pass before the Internet can safely use it.

questions: how to specify a new congestion control algorithm
how are new congestion control algorithms evaluated
can a congestion control algorithm be published as an rfc without deployment
subtitle: The checklist the IETF uses to judge a proposed congestion control algorithm, rewritten for QUIC, real-time media and algorithms already deployed at scale.

tldr.problem: Congestion control algorithms can behave badly on different paths and next to other traffic, yet algorithms such as CUBIC and BBR were deployed widely before any RFC reviewed them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out evaluation criteria for a single algorithm, for mixing with other algorithms, for general-use scenarios and for special cases, plus rules for which RFC status a specification can seek.
tldr.outcome: It is Best Current Practice 133 and obsoletes RFC 5033. It deliberately gives criteria to weigh rather than a pass or fail checklist.

facts.label: BBRv1 loss threshold
facts.value: buffer under roughly one and a half times the BDP

today: RFC 9743 is a Best Current Practice and obsoletes RFC 5033. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the current guidance for specifying new congestion control algorithms.

sections.title: Why the Guidance Was Rewritten
sections.content:
RFC 9743 gives guidelines for the IETF when it evaluates a proposed congestion control algorithm that differs from the principles in RFC 2914. It is meant for authors who propose algorithms and for the community deciding whether a proposal should be published as an RFC and deployed in the Internet. It obsoletes RFC 5033, published in 2007.

The RFC lists what changed since then. QUIC (RFC 9000) and the RTP Media Congestion Avoidance Techniques work joined TCP as users of congestion control, and interest grew in data centers and real-time protocols. Some algorithms were also deployed at scale without full IETF review. The text names CUBIC, which became the default for the Linux TCP implementation and was published as RFC 8312 and then RFC 9438, and BBR, which is described in Internet-Drafts.

The authors draw a plain conclusion: deployment of new algorithms is not gated by publication as an RFC. A specification still helps implementers, operators and contributors share an understanding of how an algorithm behaves.

The document does not give hard-and-fast requirements. It provides criteria that developers and the IETF weigh for each proposal, and it says they should not be read as a checklist to complete before approaching the IETF. Multicast congestion control is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some very popular new rules for sharing the road were already in use before anyone wrote the official guide. So the guide was updated to match how things really work today.

sections.title: Document Status and Evaluation
sections.content:
The guidelines apply to congestion control specifications seeking an RFC through the IETF Stream with Experimental or Standards Track status. Both are asked the same questions, but with different expectations for the answers.

A specification without empirical evidence of Internet-scale deployment MUST seek Experimental status, unless it is not targeted for general use. Experimental specifications SHOULD NOT be deployed as a default. They should only be deployed where they are actively measured and can be deactivated if the behavior turns pathological. A specification with a record of measured Internet-scale deployment MAY go directly to the Standards Track if solid data shows the algorithm is safe and the design stable.

Every specification is REQUIRED to state in its abstract whether there is IETF consensus that the algorithm is safe for use on the Internet, and to describe environments where it is not recommended for deployment.

Before publication as Experimental or Standards Track, the community SHOULD gain practical experience with implementations. Evaluation can start in a simulator and can use an emulated laboratory or a controlled experiment. An algorithm with a single implementation may still be published if that implementation is widely used, open source and shown to have a positive impact, especially for Experimental status.
sections.eli5: If a new rule has not been tried out on real roads yet, it gets a trial label. Only rules that have proven safe can get the full stamp of approval, and every rule must say honestly where it should not be used.

sections.title: Controlled Environments
sections.content:
An algorithm can be designed for general Internet deployment or for a controlled environment, where an operator can isolate flows from the rest of the Internet or choose to let them share resources. A data center is the example the RFC gives, often with rich signaling from switches to endpoints.

An algorithm that relies on specific functions or configuration in the network needs a reference or specification for them, such as an RFC or another stable specification. The IETF also has to consider whether a working group exists that can assess the network-layer aspects.

To evaluate such a proposal the community needs to understand how the usage is scoped, whether the algorithm shares resources with Internet traffic, and what happens if it is used in a protocol bridged across an Internet path. If an algorithm is confined to a controlled environment, the evaluation criteria in the rest of the RFC might not apply, and real-world data from that environment may matter more.
sections.eli5: A private race track can have its own rules because only the race cars drive there. But you must say clearly what happens if one of those cars drives out onto the public road.

sections.title: Single Algorithm Criteria
sections.content:
The first group of criteria looks at flows that all use the proposed algorithm and share a bottleneck link. The community MUST consider the criteria in the RFC. Where a SHOULD criterion is not met, the community MUST document whether that is acceptable.

  • Congestion collapse. The algorithm should stop sending when the packet drop rate exceeds some threshold, or include a notion of full backoff: reduce the rate to one packet per round-trip time, then exponentially back off the time between single packets if congestion persists.
  • Bufferbloat. The algorithm ought to avoid keeping excessive queues in the network. The RFC notes that Reno (RFC 5681) and CUBIC send faster until a FIFO buffer completely fills, adding latency for every connection through the bottleneck.
  • High packet loss. The algorithm needs to avoid causing excessively high loss and should reduce its rate when it sees high loss. The first version of BBR failed this: with multiple flows and a buffer smaller than roughly one and a half times the bandwidth-delay product, it caused sustained loss.
  • Fairness among its own flows. The evaluation should explore how capacity is shared, though fairness can be less useful when flows seek different rates or are short.
  • Short flows. A proposal MUST consider how new and short-lived flows affect long-lived flows and vice versa.
sections.eli5: A new rule must not let everyone jam the road, must not make cars queue for ages, must slow down when many packages go missing, must be fair between its own users, and must also work for quick trips.

sections.title: Coexisting with Other Traffic
sections.content:
The mixed-behavior criteria ask how the proposal interacts with algorithms already in use. The measure of harm is not only unequal capacity but also added latency or more packet loss. An evaluation MUST assess the potential to cause starvation, including assurance that losing all feedback, for example when a retransmission timeout expires, results in backoff.

A proposal MUST be evaluated against standard IETF congestion controls such as RFC 5681, RFC 9002 and RFC 9438. A significantly negative effect on those flows makes it suspect. The RFC says this is not a requirement for strict Reno or CUBIC friendliness, and gives HighSpeed TCP as an Experimental example that is not Reno friendly in all environments.

A proposal SHOULD also consider coexistence with widely deployed real-time congestion control algorithms. These usually have finite throughput needs and stricter latency bounds. The RFC admits that at the time of writing many widely deployed real-time algorithms have incomplete public specifications.

Two further items are MUSTs: a proposal must clearly explain deviations from RFC 2914 and RFC 7141, and it must discuss whether it allows incremental deployment in its target environment.
sections.eli5: A new kind of vehicle has to share the road with trucks, bikes and ambulances. It is tested to see that it does not squeeze the others out, and its makers must explain how it can be introduced a little at a time.

sections.title: General Use and Special Cases
sections.content:
Unless a specification explicitly forbids use on the public Internet, there MUST be IETF consensus that it meets the criteria in the general-use scenarios. Each scenario should be tested over a representative range of bandwidths, delays and queue depths. The scenarios are paths with tail-drop queues, tunnels, wired paths and wireless paths. Wireless paths matter because some losses come from radio effects rather than queue drops, and capacity and round-trip times vary.

Section 7 covers special cases. The community MAY let a proposal progress even if the result is unsatisfactory for one of them. The cases are:

  • Active queue management, such as FQ-CoDel, PIE and L4S, including reacting to ECN-CE marks.
  • Network transport circuit breakers that stop or slow a flow in excessive congestion.
  • Paths with varying or high delay, such as satellite links.
  • Internet of Things and constrained nodes, where power and CPU limit complexity.
  • Misbehaving nodes and attackers, extreme packet reordering, transient events and sudden path changes (the last one is a MUST to evaluate).
  • Multipath transport, where each path needs independent congestion control and the harm of failover or shared bottlenecks must be evaluated.
  • Data centers, with latencies below 2 ms, where a proposal need not coexist with all algorithms but SHOULD say which are expected to coexist safely.
sections.eli5: The new rule is tried on many kinds of roads: smooth ones, bumpy wireless ones, very long ones and tiny ones for small gadgets. It does not have to be perfect everywhere, but the makers must know how it behaves.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC does not change any aspect of the TCP/IP protocol suite, so it does not directly affect Internet security. It does note that the implementation of the Internet's current congestion control algorithms has security implications, as outlined in RFC 5681. A proposal MUST examine any security or privacy issues that arise from its design.

The IANA Considerations section says the document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: This guide does not change how the Internet works, so it is not a security risk by itself. Anyone proposing a new rule still has to think about how a bad person could abuse it.

items.title: Congestion collapse
items.text: Stop sending above a drop-rate threshold or use full backoff.

items.title: Bufferbloat
items.text: Avoid keeping excessive queues in the network.

items.title: High packet loss
items.text: Avoid causing high loss and cut the rate when loss is high.

items.title: Fairness
items.text: Explore how capacity is shared among its own flows.

items.title: Short flows
items.text: Consider how short and long flows affect each other.
